1.note: See how you translated **Thus says Yahweh** in 2:5. This also occurs in verses 3, 6, 11, 18, and 30 of this chapter.

1.q: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה רֵ֖ד בֵּֽית־מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה וְ⁠דִבַּרְתָּ֣ שָׁ֔ם אֶת־הַ⁠דָּבָ֖ר הַ⁠זֶּֽה
1.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh told me that I should go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:11.

2.note: Jeremiah is using **And you shall say** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation of the message that Yahweh is giving him to speak, and that it comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you should tell him to hear the word of Yahweh, he who is king of Judah]
See how you translated this phrase in 2:4. This also occurs in verse 29.
See how you translated this expression in 17:25. This also occurs in verse 30.

The pronoun **your** refers to the king of Judah, whom Yahweh is telling Jeremiah to address. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. This also occurs in verse 4. Alternate translation: [and your servants and your people, king of Judah]

3.note: The terms **justice** and **righteousness** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. This also occurs in verse 15. Alternate translation: [what is completely right]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **justice** and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [what is just and right]

The expression **the one who has been robbed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the one whom someone has robbed]

Here, **hand** represents the power that a person has over someone else. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the control of the oppressor]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [act violently]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **oppress**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [And protect the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **violence**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [Act peacefully, and do not shed innocent blood]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:6.

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [Do not harm anyone by killing innocent people]

4.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that kings will continue to rule in Jerusalem only if the king and his people obey this command. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If you truly obey this command]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **do** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you certainly do]

Here, **throne** represents the royal authority of the king who sits on it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [kings who rule as David’s successors]

The pronoun **he** refers to each one of the **kings** whom Yahweh has just mentioned. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [each of those kings, along with his servants and his people]

5.note: Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between what he has just said would happen if the king obeys him and what he says here will happen if the king does not obey him. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [On the other hand,]

Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that this house will become a ruin if the king and his people do not obey this command. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [But if it happens that you do not obey these words]

Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by himself, since there is no one greater by whom he could swear. He is doing this to guarantee that what he says will certainly happen. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I solemnly promise on my own authority]
See how you translated **the declaration of Yahweh** in 1:8. This also occurs in verses 16 and 24.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **a ruin**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [completely ruined]

6.q: כִּֽי־כֹ֣ה ׀ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה עַל־בֵּית֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה
6.note: Jeremiah is using **thus says Yahweh** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the royal house of Judah were **Gilead** and **the top of Lebanon**, regions that were known for their fine forests. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You are as splendid to me as the forests of Gilead, as the heights of Lebanon]

6.q: אִם־לֹ֤א אֲשִֽׁיתְ⁠ךָ֙ מִדְבָּ֔ר עָרִ֖ים לֹ֥א נושבה
6.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the royal house of Judah were **a wilderness** and **cities not inhabited**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But surely I will leave you ruined and empty of people]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will make you cities not inhabited]

The expression **not inhabited** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [cities where nobody lives]

7.note: The pronoun **you** refers to the royal house of Judah, which Yahweh has been addressing since the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [against you, house of the king of Judah]

Yahweh is using **a man and his weapons** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each one of them with his own weapons.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each one of them armed with his own weapons]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the finest parts of the royal house of Judah were **the choicest of your cedars**, continuing the image of a forest from the previous verse. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who are like your choicest cedars]

8.note: Jeremiah is using **a man to his neighbor** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each one of them to another.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each one to another]

8.q: עַל־מֶ֨ה עָשָׂ֤ה יְהוָה֙ כָּ֔כָה לָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠גְּדוֹלָ֖ה הַ⁠זֹּֽאת
8.note: The people of the nations are using the question form to express their shock at what has happened to this city. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We cannot believe that Yahweh has done this to such a great city!]

8.q: וְ⁠אָֽמְרוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֔⁠הוּ עַל־מֶ֨ה עָשָׂ֤ה יְהוָה֙ כָּ֔כָה לָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠גְּדוֹלָ֖ה הַ⁠זֹּֽאת
8.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and they will say to each other that they do not know why Yahweh had done such a thing to this great city.]

The ULT reflects the word order of the original language here. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the word **this** before the word **great**. Alternate translation: [to this great city]

9.q: וְ⁠אָ֣מְר֔וּ עַ֚ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָֽזְב֔וּ אֶת־בְּרִ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠הֶ֑ם וַ⁠יִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֛וּ לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֥ים אֲחֵרִ֖ים וַ⁠יַּעַבְדֽוּ⁠ם
9.note: The words translated as **On account of the fact that** indicate that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And they will say, ‘They abandoned the covenant of Yahweh their God and bowed down to other gods and served them; that is why he did this.’]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Judah, not to the people of the nations who are speaking. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Judah abandoned]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what they had solemnly agreed with Yahweh]

10.note: The pronoun **him** refers to the dead one, that is, to King Josiah, who has died. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for the one who has died]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **weep** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Weep profusely]

The expression **the one going away** refers to King Shallum, who is being taken away into exile, and **the dead one** refers to his father, King Josiah, who has died. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for King Shallum, who is going into exile]

11.note: Jeremiah is using **thus says Yahweh** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.
The word **Shallum** is the name of a man. He was a king of Judah who was also known as Jehoahaz.

11.q: הַ⁠מֹּלֵךְ֙ תַּ֚חַת יֹאשִׁיָּ֣הוּ אָבִ֔י⁠ו אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָצָ֖א מִן־הַ⁠מָּק֣וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה
11.note: Here Jeremiah is providing background information to help readers understand what follows. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

12.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the foreign rulers who took King Shallum away from Judah, and the pronoun **him** refers to Shallum. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [where his foreign captors exiled Shallum]

13.note: Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of sorrow and condemnation. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible it will be for the one building his house by unrighteousness]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the house that this king is building for himself. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a house for himself by acting unrighteously]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **unrighteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by acting unrighteously]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **injustice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by acting unjustly]

13.q: בְּ⁠רֵעֵ֨⁠הוּ֙ יַעֲבֹ֣ד חִנָּ֔ם וּ⁠פֹעֲל֖⁠וֹ לֹ֥א יִתֶּן־לֽ⁠וֹ
13.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [who forces his neighbor to work without paying him anything for it]

14.note: The word **vermilion** refers to a kind of bright red pigment that people used as paint. If your readers would not be familiar with what vermilion is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with red paint]

15.note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the king for supposing that a fine palace is what makes a man a king. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Having more cedar than everyone else certainly does not make you a king!]

15.q: אָבִ֜י⁠ךָ הֲ⁠ל֧וֹא אָכַ֣ל וְ⁠שָׁתָ֗ה וְ⁠עָשָׂ֤ה מִשְׁפָּט֙ וּ⁠צְדָקָ֔ה
15.note: Yahweh is using the question form to remind the king of the way his father Josiah ruled. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Your father ate and drank, and he also did justice and righteousness.]

Yahweh is using **eat and drink** as a common expression of the culture to mean “enjoy the good things of life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [enjoy the good things of life]

16.note: Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the legal cases that belonged to **the poor and the needy**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the legal cases that poor and needy people brought]

Jeremiah is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [poor and needy people]

The terms **the poor** and **the needy** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the very destitute]

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that treating people justly is what it means to know him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This is surely what it means to know me!]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean knowing him personally and doing what he requires. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what it means to know me]

17.note: Yahweh’s speech resumes here after Jeremiah interrupted it at the end of the previous verse in order to attest that Yahweh was the one speaking. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Here, **your eyes** represent what a person pays attention to and desires. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your attention]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the thoughts and desires of Jehoiakim were in **your heart**. In this culture, people spoke of the heart as the place where a person thinks and wants things. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your thoughts and desires are not on anything]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **unjust gain**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what you unjustly gain]

Here, **the blood of the innocent** represents the murder of people who have done nothing wrong. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and upon the murder of innocent people to carry it out]

The terms **oppression** and **extortion** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [violent acts of exploitation]

18.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 18:13.

Jeremiah is using **thus says Yahweh** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

The pronoun **They** refers to the people of Judah in general, and the pronoun **him** refers to Jehoiakim. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people of Judah will not mourn for Jehoiakim]

18.q: ה֥וֹי אָחִ֖⁠י וְ⁠ה֣וֹי אָח֑וֹת לֹא־יִסְפְּד֣וּ ל֔⁠וֹ ה֥וֹי אָד֖וֹן וְ⁠ה֥וֹי הֹדֹֽ⁠ה
18.note: Yahweh is using phrases that express a strong feeling of grief. These were the cries that people of this culture customarily used when they mourned for someone who had died. There may be equivalent words or phrases in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [saying, ‘How terrible, my brother!’ and ‘How terrible, sister!’ They will not mourn for him, saying, ‘How terrible, master!’ and ‘How terrible, his majesty!’]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [saying that they lament for their brother and for their sister]

19.note: Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

The expression **He will be buried** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People will bury him]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the burial**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as people bury a donkey]

The expression **dragged and thrown out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with people dragging him and throwing him out]

The terms **dragged** and **thrown out** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [hauled away like trash]

20.note: In keeping with what was usual in the biblical language and culture, the speaker is indicating that people would be going up to a higher elevation if they were to travel as he describes. If your language does not mark travel for change in elevation, you can translate this and similar instances with simple expressions such as “go” or “come.” Alternate translation: [Go to Lebanon]

Yahweh is speaking to the city of Jerusalem, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the judgment that is coming on the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [Go up to Lebanon, you people of Jerusalem, and cry out]
See how you translated this phrase in 2:15.

The pronoun **your** refers to the city of Jerusalem, which Yahweh is addressing as if it were a woman. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the voice of Jerusalem]
The word **Abarim** is the name of a range of mountains east of the Jordan River.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the nations that were allied with Judah were **your lovers**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 22. Alternate translation: [all your allies are broken]

The expression **are broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [enemies have broken all your lovers]

21.note: The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh, and the pronoun **you** refers to the city of Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, spoke to you people of Jerusalem]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prosperity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when you were prospering]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [you said that you would not hear]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the habitual conduct of the people of Jerusalem were **your way**, that is, a road on which they walked. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has been how you have habitually behaved since your youth]

22.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if **The wind** were a shepherd who would drive **all your shepherds** away. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The wind shall blow all your shepherds away]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the leaders of Jerusalem were **shepherds** who cared for the people as a flock. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your rulers]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as captives]
See how you translated the similar expression in 14:3.

The expression **humiliated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and other nations will humiliate you]

23.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Jerusalem were birds **nesting in the cedars** of Lebanon, possibly referring to their comfortable homes built of the cedar wood imported from Lebanon.. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You who live in Lebanon, you who make your homes secure among the cedars]

The expression **you will be pitied** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [how people will pity you]

The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “you will be pitied.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “you will groan.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **pangs** and **pain**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [when you begin to suffer sharply, hurting]
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:24.

24.note: Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by his own life in order to guarantee that what he says will certainly happen. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I swear by my own life]

24.q: כִּ֣י אִם־יִהְיֶ֞ה כָּנְיָ֤הוּ בֶן־יְהֽוֹיָקִים֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה חוֹתָ֖ם עַל־יַ֣ד יְמִינִ֑⁠י
24.note: Yahweh is making a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. He is stating it as a condition to show that nothing could keep him from removing Coniah from being king. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [even if Coniah, the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a signet on my right hand, which he is not]
The word **Coniah** is the name of a man. It is a shortened form of the name Jeconiah, and this king was also called Jehoiachin. This also occurs in verse 28.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Coniah were **a signet on my right hand**, a ring that a ruler wore and used to mark documents with his own authority. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [were as close to me as the ring of authority on my right hand]

The pronoun **you** refers to Coniah. Yahweh has been speaking about him, but here he begins to speak directly to him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I would tear you off, Coniah]

25.note: Yahweh is using **the ones seeking your life** as a common expression of the culture to mean those who want to kill someone. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones hunting for your life] or [the ones who want to kill you]

Yahweh is using **from their face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are terrified of]

Here, **hand** represents power and control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and under the control of the Chaldeans]

26.note: The expression **you were not born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [where your mother did not give birth to you]

It might seem that the expression **and your mother who bore you** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and your mother]

27.note: The pronoun **they** refers to Coniah and his mother. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these two are lifting up their soul]

Yahweh is using **lifting up their soul** as a common expression of the culture to mean “longing for something.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are longing with all their heart]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **return** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [they will certainly not return there]

28.q: הַ⁠עֶ֨צֶב נִבְזֶ֜ה נָפ֗וּץ הָ⁠אִ֤ישׁ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ כָּנְיָ֔הוּ אִ֨ם־כְּלִ֔י אֵ֥ין חֵ֖פֶץ בּ֑⁠וֹ
28.note: Here Jeremiah is speaking as if Coniah were **a despised, shattered vessel** that no one valued. 28.q: הַ⁠עֶ֨צֶב נִבְזֶ֜ה נָפ֗וּץ הָ⁠אִ֤ישׁ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ כָּנְיָ֔הוּ
28.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to express that people regard Coniah as worthless. 28.q: הַ⁠עֶ֨צֶב נִבְזֶ֜ה נָפ֗וּץ הָ⁠אִ֤ישׁ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ כָּנְיָ֔הוּ

28.q: מַדּ֤וּעַ הֽוּטֲלוּ֙ ה֣וּא וְ⁠זַרְע֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠הֻ֨שְׁלְכ֔וּ עַל־הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹא־יָדָֽעוּ
